A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same labelled-sample break-even study despite the changed title and expanded scope. Text, figures, tables and v1's Appendices A–D support reliable comparison; much appendix material is reorganized into v2's main text.

before.justification: v1 reports original macro-F1 experiments and break-even thresholds on SST-2, MRPC and BoolQ, plus sample-selection and instruction-tuning ablations in Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 reports original comparisons across eight datasets and seven language models, including performance curves, variability and break-even thresholds in Figures 1–2 and Table 2.

M1.justification: The four-approach framework remains, but instruction-tuning gains a procedural extension: v1 fully tunes Flan-T5, while v2 additionally uses LoRA to instruction-tune Mistral-7B and Zephyr-7B. This is a limited adaptation within the existing framework.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from three binary datasets to eight classification datasets. CoLA adds grammatical acceptability, while AG News, TREC, SNIPS and DB Pedia add news, question, intent and topic classification with 4–14 classes. SST-2, MRPC and BoolQ remain.

E2.justification: Mistral-7B and Zephyr-7B become evaluated comparators in prompting, in-context learning and instruction-tuning, including on the retained datasets. Figure 2 verifies their participation alongside the original BERT, RoBERTa, Flan-T5, LLaMA-2 and ChatGPT models.

E3.justification: The reported split changes from 80:20 training/test to 60:20:20 training/validation/test. Fine-tuning changes from Adam with 5 or 10 epochs to AdamW with warmup and a maximum of 10 epochs. Flan-T5 instruction-tuning changes from 150 fixed steps to five epochs capped at 250 steps each with early stopping. Prompt formats and selection also change, and generation limits increase from 4 to 10 tokens. These specifications do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v1's random-versus-similarity example-selection experiment and four instruction-tuning schedule/batch comparisons disappear with Figures 3–4. v2 retains only a brief overfitting explanation for the training constraint and adds a qualitative DB Pedia failure investigation involving class-count reduction. The central break-even and variance analyses largely survive through reorganization.

E5.justification: The reported repetition regime changes substantially: v1 specifies 100 runs for most approaches and six for ChatGPT; v2 retains 100 for fine-tuning, specifies 20 for other approaches and increases ChatGPT to ten. Mean macro-F1, standard deviation and shared-seed reporting remain. Variance-aware break-even comparisons already existed in v1 Appendix C.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for the new datasets and models, plus an empirical aggregate in Figure 1. Retained thresholds also change: Table 2 reports 80 versus 90 labels for BERT to exceed Flan-T5 prompting on SST-2 in v1 versus v2. A new BoolQ comparison reports 500 versus 8000 labels for BERT to exceed Mistral/Zephyr in-context learning before versus after accounting for variance. Changed protocols preclude interpreting version differences as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs. v2's first and second break-even points restate the average-performance and standard-deviation distinction already explained in v1 Appendix C, without a substantive mathematical revision.

C1.justification: The central benefit of specialization remains, but v2 adds a binary-versus-multiclass claim and changes the abstract's typical label range from 100–1000 to 10–1000. The claimed variance penalty expands from v1's 25–200% to 100–200% on average and up to 1500%. Practical recommendations become an explicit contribution, building on advice already present in v1's appendix.

C2.justification: v2 develops class-count and input-characteristic interpretations beyond v1's mainly task-complexity framing. It discusses DB Pedia's single-class prediction failure and LoRA versus full tuning as a possible variance confound. Section 3.4 expands existing prototyping advice into annotation/computation-budget recommendations. Limitations shift from excluding multiclass tasks to broader classification-only generalization concerns and acknowledge prompt selection using Mistral.

D1.justification: v2 condenses the technical documentation, omitting v1 Appendix B's exact batch-size mapping, inference batch size of 64, invalid-output scoring rule and refinement procedure around break-even points. It documents four-bit use for Mistral/Zephyr and updates compute accounting from 2000 to 4000 A100 hours and estimated emissions from 216 to 432 kgCO2eq. The source-code address is unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands its treatment of model-size comparisons, approach coverage and sensitivity to randomness, including new discussion of Ma et al. and Liu et al. Additional model, dataset and prompt-sensitivity works are cited, while several RLHF-background references disappear. Publication updates to Chung et al. and the clinical-language-model paper represent retained works.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v1's dataset-by-dataset results and lengthy Appendix C discussion become research-question and theme-based Sections 3.1–3.4. Experimental details are condensed into Section 3, and ethics and compute-impact material move from appendices to the main document.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from a schematic to an empirical aggregate, and Figure 2 is redesigned from three panels into paired prompting/ICL panels for eight datasets. Separate appendix figures disappear. Table 1 becomes a shared prompt template with dataset verbalisers; Table 2 replaces individual-model/training-fraction entries with model-size groups, paired break-even thresholds and percentage increases.

improvement.justification: The broader evidence addresses v1's acknowledged restriction to three binary datasets, and Table 2 makes average and variance-aware thresholds easier to compare. The net gain is limited by removed ablations and implementation details, fewer repetitions for most retained comparison methods, and an overbroad new claim: Section 3.1 states that multiclass break-even requires at most 100 labels, whereas Table 2 reports 350 for RoBERTa and 550 for BERT against Flan-T5 in-context learning on AG News.
